title: Encouraging Others to View Critical Feedback as a Reward
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article argues that whether feedback lands as a punishment or a reward depends heavily on how leaders frame it, not just its content. Using three sample phrasings of the same underlying suggestion, the author shows how emphasizing past progress before offering new critical input reframes feedback as evidence of growth rather than a fresh critique. The piece closes on the idea that reminding people of prior improvement makes them hungrier for more feedback, effectively training an appetite for critical input.
points: Whether feedback is experienced as a reward or a punishment depends heavily on how it's framed, not just what is said.
Opening with acknowledgment of progress already made from earlier feedback reframes new criticism as part of a growth story, not a fresh complaint.
A pure critique statement reads as judgment, while a statement tied to visible past improvement reads as development.
Reminding people that past feedback already helped them improve builds an appetite for more feedback going forward.
quotes: Those team members fixated on improving actively seek feedback and view it as a reward.
Over time, whether feedback is seen as a reward or a punishment comes down to what leaders emphasize when they offer it.
The last statement emphasizes the progress made by following earlier feedback and then offers some more.
Leaders who want team members to seek feedback and find it rewarding underline how others have already benefited from feedback in the past.
This is yet another example that what leaders feed people determines their appetite.
